strengths: Introduces a novel mechanistic interpretability approach to typographic attacks in CLIP, identifying specialized attention heads and using training-free circuit ablation for defense.
Scales cleanly across CLIP model sizes from ViT-B to ViT-BigG, showing that sparse typographic circuits exist even at billion-parameter scale.
Reports consistent improvements on multiple typographic attack datasets while keeping non-typographic accuracy degradation near 1%.
Provides causal manipulation experiments and layer-wise linear probes, offering useful evidence for the causal role of selected heads.
Releases a family of dyslexic CLIP models as practical drop-in replacements for safety-critical settings.
weaknesses: The Typographic Attention Score in Eq. 6 appears mathematically problematic: the numerator and denominator both contain A^*_{i,l}(x)_t, so the score cancels to a head-independent constant unless a normalization term is missing. This undermines clarity and reproducibility of the core head-ranking method.

The circuit construction algorithm is greedy and stops at the first head that violates the accuracy constraint, rather than continuing to evaluate lower-ranked heads; it also optimizes only non-typographic accuracy and does not directly validate typographic robustness during construction.

Evaluation compares against only Defense-Prefix, and DP outperforms the proposed method on most typographic benchmarks; the claim of being competitive with state-of-the-art typographic defenses is overstated.

There is no random-head ablation control, no statistical significance testing or error bars on the small typographic datasets, and the causal attention-manipulation experiment does not compare against non-circuit heads.

The Typographic Attention Score is computed on Unsplash-Typo with text fixed at bottom-center, but the defense is evaluated on attacks with varying and random text locations; generalization of the score to arbitrary text locations is not thoroughly analyzed.

The defense only modifies the CLS token residual stream and leaves spatial tokens untouched, which limits applicability to VLMs and downstream multimodal systems that use patch tokens; this limitation is acknowledged but not empirically addressed.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or model release links are provided, and key details such as probe train/test splits, exact head-selection hyperparameters, and failure cases are not fully specified.

The manuscript contains clarity issues, including typos/inconsistent spelling ('dislexic', 'behaivor', 'casual'), ambiguous notation around circuit ablation, and an equation that is likely misprinted.

strengths: Provides a mechanistic interpretability angle for typographic attacks in CLIP by attempting to localize attention heads that transmit typographic information to the CLS token.
The training-free circuit ablation is computationally attractive and is evaluated across multiple OpenCLIP scales, from ViT-B to ViT-BigG.
Reports large improvements on a synthetic ImageNet-100-Typo benchmark (up to 19.6%) with relatively small drops on standard ImageNet-100 accuracy.
Includes evaluations on several real-world typographic datasets and releases a family of robust model variants, which could be useful if the method is validated.
weaknesses: The core Typographic Attention Score in Eq. 6 is mathematically problematic: the numerator and denominator both contain the same attention term, so the expression simplifies to counting typographic tokens rather than producing a normalized score in [0,1]. The intended normalization over total spatial attention mass appears to be missing, undermining the head-ranking and circuit construction.

Circuit construction relies on a 5% ImageNet-100 train split and an accuracy-drop threshold, but the evaluation split is unclear. This risks selection overfitting and makes the claimed minimal standard-accuracy drop less convincing.

Baselines are insufficient. Only Defense-Prefix is compared, and it outperforms the proposed method on most typographic datasets. Missing comparisons include PAINT, Disentangling, fine-tuning/robust fine-tuning, SAE steering, random head ablation, attention pruning, and simple inference-time defenses.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are reported. Several real-world typographic evaluation sets are very small (e.g., PAINT-DS and Disentangling), so the reported improvements may not be reliable.

The causal evidence is not fully convincing: manipulating CLS-to-CLS attention and rescaling all spatial attention is not equivalent to selective circuit ablation, and it does not isolate typographic tokens from other spatial information.

The defense only modifies the CLS token residual stream, while many downstream VLMs and adapters rely on spatial tokens. The paper acknowledges this limitation but still claims broad drop-in replacement suitability without evaluating VLMs or downstream safety tasks.

Text-recognition utility is not evaluated. A model that is intentionally less sensitive to typographic text may fail on OCR, retrieval, or safety-critical tasks that require reading text, so the safety-versus-utility tradeoff is not adequately quantified.
The term 'dyslexic' for the model family is unnecessary and potentially stigmatizing; this terminology should be reconsidered.
Reproducibility is limited: no code link or checkpoint details are provided, and key experimental choices such as exact train/validation/test splits and threshold sensitivity are not fully specified.

Writing and presentation quality are weak, with multiple typos and notation errors (e.g., 'casual' for causal, 'dislexic', inconsistent dataset naming), which makes the technical claims harder to trust.

strengths: Identifies specialized attention heads in CLIP vision encoders that affect typographic attacks using linear probes and a Typographic Attention Score, adding mechanistic interpretability to an important robustness problem.

The training-free circuit-ablation method improves robustness across model scales and multiple typographic datasets, with up to 19.6% improvement on ImageNet-100-Typo while maintaining standard zero-shot accuracy within roughly 1%.
The approach scales to billion-parameter OpenCLIP models without fine-tuning, which is practical and computationally efficient.
Causal manipulation of attention patterns supports the claim that the selected heads transfer typographic information to the CLS token.
The paper releases a family of dyslexic CLIP models and demonstrates a reasonable robustness/accuracy trade-off, with competitive non-typographic performance relative to Defense-Prefix.
weaknesses: Eq. (6) for the Typographic Attention Score appears mathematically invalid as written: if A* appears in both numerator and denominator inside the sum, T reduces to counting typographic tokens and cannot produce the reported head-specific percentages or rankings. This needs correction and clarification.

Missing control experiments: there is no comparison to random-head ablation, magnitude-matched head ablation, or alternative head-ranking criteria, so it remains unclear whether the gains are specific to typographic heads or simply due to ablating later-layer heads.

Baseline comparison is limited to Defense-Prefix. Defense-Prefix outperforms the proposed method on most typographic benchmarks, which weakens the claim that the method is competitive with state-of-the-art typographic defenses.

Circuit construction is greedy and terminates at the first head that degrades accuracy. There is no ablation over ranking order, epsilon, or circuit size, so the resulting circuits may be brittle or suboptimal.

The Typographic Attention Score is computed on Unsplash-Typo with fixed bottom-center text, while real attacks use varied positions and styles. Generalization to location and appearance variation is not fully isolated.
Evaluation on some typographic datasets is small (e.g., 180 examples for Disentangling, 110 for PAINT-DS) and lacks error bars or statistical significance tests.
The manuscript contains several typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'dislexic', 'casual' for causal, 'behaivor'), which reduce clarity in an otherwise technical paper.

strengths: Provides a mechanistic interpretability analysis of CLIP under typographic attacks, identifying later-layer attention heads with spatially biased attention to typographic regions using a Typographic Attention Score.
Introduces a gradient-free circuit-ablation defense, Dyslexify, that can be applied to CLIP models up to billion-parameter scale without fine-tuning and with low memory overhead.
Demonstrates empirical robustness gains across multiple CLIP model sizes and typographic datasets, with reported standard ImageNet-100 accuracy drops mostly within ~1%.
Extends the analysis to a safety-critical medical foundation model, showing typographic attacks can reduce melanoma-detection accuracy and that the proposed defense can mitigate this.
Releases dyslexic CLIP models and code, and transparently reports OCR degradation and computational/memory comparisons.
The method is computationally lighter than Defense-Prefix on several models and requires only forward passes and accuracy evaluations rather than gradient-based training.
weaknesses: The baseline comparison is insufficient: only Defense-Prefix is compared in the main tables, while a simple OCR+blur preprocessing baseline in Appendix J consistently outperforms Dyslexify on ImageNet-100-Typo across model sizes, weakening the claim of being competitive with state-of-the-art typographic defenses.

No adaptive-attack evaluation is provided. The paper argues adaptive attacks are infeasible because typographic attacks are non-differentiable, but black-box, transfer-based, or search-based adaptive attacks remain plausible and are necessary evidence for a defense paper.

Circuit construction requires paired clean and typographic data, and the Typographic Attention Score relies on known spatial typographic region masks; this limits practical deployment and is not fully addressed for arbitrary new domains.

The defense only modifies the CLS token path, leaving spatial tokens untouched; this limits applicability to VLMs and diffusion/adapters that use spatial tokens, as the authors note but do not evaluate beyond standard CLS-based classification.

Several technical and clarity issues remain: inconsistent/duplicated equation numbering, contradictory wording around alpha in Figure 5, typos, unclear dataset splits, and missing statistical significance or variance estimates for main results.

The evaluation lacks comparisons to other typographic defenses mentioned in related work (e.g., Materzynska et al., sparse autoencoders, fine-tuning/weight interpolation), and lacks ablations over key design choices such as ranking score, epsilon, and skip threshold k.

Claims such as 'drop-in replacements' and 'first causal intervention' are somewhat overstated given that OCR+blur is stronger on the main synthetic benchmark and downstream VLM/generative evaluations are absent.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: typographic attacks on CLIP and multimodal systems.
Mechanistic analysis using linear probes to localize typographic understanding and an attention-based score to identify candidate typographic heads is interesting and interpretable.
Proposes a gradient-free intervention that does not fine-tune CLIP, ablates a sparse circuit of attention heads, and can be applied to billion-parameter models.

Evaluates across multiple model sizes and datasets, including real-world typo benchmarks, synthetic typo datasets, and a medical foundation model, with reported robustness gains and limited clean accuracy loss.
Releases a dyslexic CLIP model family and discusses limitations and ethical/misuse considerations.
weaknesses: A simple OCR+blur baseline in Appendix J consistently outperforms Dyslexify on ImageNet-100-Typo across model sizes while preserving clean accuracy, directly weakening the central defense claim. This baseline is not in the main text and is dismissed without sufficient justification.

The empirical comparison is too limited: only Defense-Prefix on ViT-L is compared in the main paper; no other typographic defenses (e.g., projection-matrix, weight interpolation/patching, SAE steering) are evaluated. The claim of being competitive with state-of-the-art defenses is not supported.

The circuit-ablation technically only zeros the CLS-token contribution of selected heads while leaving their spatial-token updates unchanged. Typographic information written into spatial tokens could still be read by later CLS attention, so the method may not fully ablate the claimed circuit.

Adaptive/realistic attack evaluation is insufficient. The paper uses fixed synthetic fonts/locations and does not test variation in text location, font, size, multiple text regions, rendering, or black-box/transfer-based attacks. The claim that adaptive attacks are infeasible because typographic attacks are non-differentiable is unconvincing.

Circuit construction requires a labeled typographic dataset in the target domain and a spatial mask of typographic content to compute T_{i,l}; it is unclear how this would be obtained for real-world attacks where text location is unknown.
Reported clean-accuracy trade-off contradicts the stated tolerance: ViT-L drops 1.74% on Aircraft and 1.17% on Food-101, exceeding the epsilon=1% criterion, while the text claims drops below 1%.

There are inconsistencies and writing issues: abstract says up to 22.06% robustness gain while results report up to 31.11%; duplicate equation numbering; typos such as 'gadient-free', 'casual nature', 'Poject page', etc.
Dyslexify severely degrades OCR performance by 8-30 points, which challenges the 'drop-in replacement' framing for applications that may require any text recognition.
The medical use-case relies on synthetic typographic overlays and does not establish realistic attack prevalence or robustness against adaptive medical-domain manipulations.

Reproducibility artifacts are only partially promised; project/code links are missing from the manuscript, and some experimental details (e.g., exact evaluation splits, probe training details, blur/OCR baseline integration) are relegated to appendices.

strengths: Introduces a novel mechanistic analysis of typographic attacks in CLIP, identifying typographic attention heads with a new Typographic Attention Score and demonstrating their causal role via controlled interventions.
Proposes a gradient-free circuit-ablation defense (Dyslexify) that requires no finetuning and scales to billion-parameter CLIP models.
Extensive empirical evaluation across five CLIP model sizes, multiple synthetic and real typographic benchmarks, plus a medical melanoma detection use case.
Shows substantial robustness gains (up to 22%+ on ImageNet-100-Typo) with small degradation on standard datasets, and releases dyslexic CLIP models.
Good reproducibility with open-sourced code and detailed appendix, including runtime/memory and OCR degradation analysis.
weaknesses: The defense is not clearly state-of-the-art: an OCR+blur preprocessing baseline in Appendix J consistently outperforms Dyslexify on ImageNet-100-Typo across model sizes, and Defense-Prefix is stronger on some datasets (e.g., Disentangling), weakening the practical claim.

Limited baseline comparison: only Defense-Prefix is compared in the main paper; other typographic defenses (disentangling projection, sparse autoencoder steering, finetuning/patching) are not evaluated.

Adaptive attacks are dismissed as infeasible due to non-differentiability, but black-box or expectation-over-transformation optimizations could target the selected circuit or attention sinks; an adaptive evaluation is expected for adversarial defenses.

Figure 5's caption/text have an apparent inconsistency: Eq. 10 defines alpha as the CLS-to-CLS attention, so increasing alpha should reduce spatial attention and typographic understanding, while the caption states increasing alpha raises spatial attention and amplifies typographic understanding. This should be corrected.

Circuit construction uses typographic labels and evaluates gains on typographic datasets; for ImageNet-100-Typo and ISIC2019-T, it is not fully clear whether the same data splits are used for circuit selection and final evaluation, raising potential overfitting/leakage concerns.
The method only modifies the CLS token and is thus limited for VLMs/downstream tasks that use spatial tokens, as acknowledged; the broader impact on full multimodal systems is not demonstrated.

Some presentation issues: appendix mentions 'Following the reviewer's suggestion,' inconsistent citation formatting, and minor typos ('Poject page', 'gadient-free'), suggesting the submission may not be fully anonymized/clean.
